citations.desc: Attending veterinarian and adequate veterinary care (dealers and exhibitors).
citations.narrative:
The facility failed to follow up with the attending veterinarian when requested to. USDA inspectors observed a male
capybara named Leonardo, with yellow mucous discharge coming from his right nostril. When inspectors asked about his
condition, the licensee said the animal was on medication from the attending veterinarian (AV) and that the animal
sometimes has this discharge and the AV did not know what it was. The USDA inspectors spoke to the AV and learned
that the licensee had been instructed to report the animal’s condition after completing the prescribed medication,
particularly if the symptoms reappeared, as further diagnostic testing would be necessary. The AV reported that no follow
up communication has been received from the licensee since July 16, 2026.
Follow up communication is essential for protecting an animal’s health and well being, especially when symptoms return.
Ongoing updates allow the veterinarian to reassess the situation quickly, determine whether a treatment plan is working,
and identify new or worsening issues before they escalate. When owners or caretakers report recurring signs promptly, it
ensures timely intervention, prevents complications, and supports a more accurate understanding of the animal’s
condition and ensures the animal receives the most effective care possible.
Each dealer or exhibitor shall establish and maintain programs of adequate veterinary care that include the use of
appropriate methods to prevent, control, diagnose, and treat diseases and injuries, and the availability of emergency,
weekend, and holiday care.

There is a buildup of dried fecal matter on the structures in the Black & White and Red Ruff lemur enclosures. In both
enclosures, small plastic tables and chairs, and a cloth hammock had accumulation of dried fecal matter that was more
than 24 hours old.
Failing to maintain clean conditions in areas accessible to nonhuman primates can lead to significant accumulations of
debris and contaminants, increasing the risk of disease and compromising the health and welfare of the animals housed
there.
Hard surfaces with which nonhuman primates come in contact must be spot cleaned daily and sanitized in accordance
with 3.84 of this subpart to prevent accumulation of excreta or disease hazards. Contaminated material must be removed
or replaced whenever raking and spot cleaning does not eliminate odors, diseases, insects, pests, or vermin infestation.

citations.desc: Cleaning, sanitization, housekeeping, and pest control.
citations.narrative:
The facility does not currently maintain an effective pest control program. There is a large quantity of rodent droppings in
the garage that acts as the main food prep and storage area for the facility. While the facility does set traps, it is not
effective in managing the rodent population.
Pests such as rodents and insects can introduce pathogens, parasites, and environmental contaminants that pose direct
health risks to animals. Contaminated feed or water can also diminish animal welfare, reduce nutritional quality, and
create stressful or unsafe living conditions.
An effective program for control of insects, external parasites affecting nonhuman primates, and birds and mammals that
are pests, must be established and maintained so as to promote the health and well- being of the animals and reduce
contamination by pests in animal areas.

The facility failed to keep two wooden structures and a wooden fence in good repair in the capybara enclosure. Two
wooden structures have exposed nail points, pushed out wooden boards, and broken pieces creating sharp points. The
posts supporting one of the structures are starting to rot. The fence separating the capybara from a tortoise yard has
broken wooden boards and sharp points.
Failure to adequately maintain primary enclosures places animals at significant risk. Structural defects or poor upkeep can
result in preventable injuries, opportunities for escape, or even death of the animals housed within.
The facility must be constructed of such material and of such strength as appropriate for the animals involved. The indoor
and outdoor housing facilities shall be structurally sound and shall be maintained in good repair to protect the animals
from injury and to contain the animals.

The facility has failed to clean the pool in the Capybara enclosure. The facility has a bathtub that serves as a pool for two
Capybaras. The pool has murky, brownish-yellow water and scattered surface debris with filamentous algae growing on
the surface of the water. Green algae is also present along the water’s edge.
Dirty water can harbor bacteria, parasites, and algae that lead to skin, eye, and gastrointestinal infections. Poor water
quality can increase stress, especially for species that rely on swimming for comfort, exercise, or cooling.
Cleaning of Enclosures. Excreta shall be removed from primary enclosures as often as necessary to prevent
contamination of the animals contained therein and to minimize disease hazards and to reduce odors. When enclosures
are cleaned by hosing or flushing, adequate measures shall be taken to protect the animals confined in such enclosures
from being directly sprayed with the stream of water or wetted involuntarily. Correct this day, August 12, 2026, forward.

The facility has a build up of dirt, debris, trash, and clutter in the room used for food prep and food storage. There is
debris, trash, old cat food cans all surrounding the containers used to store dry food for the animals. One container
holding food pellets for the Capybara has cobwebs in it. There are two baskets of rotting fruit on a shelf underneath the
counter being used to prepare fruit and vegetable diets. There is multiple areas of clutter throughout the room.
Maintaining a clean, uncluttered food prep and storage area is essential for animal welfare. Clutter and trash increase the
risk of contamination, attract pests, and compromise food safety. Improper food handling can directly affect the health of
multiple species, making strict sanitation practices critical.
Housekeeping. Premises (buildings and grounds) shall be kept clean and in good repair in order to protect the animals
from injury and to facilitate the prescribed husbandry practices set forth in this subpart. Accumulations of trash shall be
placed in designated areas and cleared as necessary to protect the health of the animals. Correct by August 19, 2026.
This inspection and exit interview were conducted with the facility representative.
Additional Inspectors:
Colette Kirk El-Amin, Supervisory Animal Care Specialist n
